entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Paolo di Campofregoso (1428–1498) was a prominent Genoese aristocrat, three-time Doge of the Republic of Genoa, and a powerful Roman Catholic Cardinal, embodying the complex interplay of secular and ecclesiastical power in Renaissance Italy. His career, spanning from 1453 as Archbishop of Genoa until his death, was marked by relentless political maneuvering, military command, and deep involvement in the factional struggles that defined the Republic's volatile independence. He navigated the treacherous waters of Italian politics, frequently clashing with rival families like the Adorno and contending with the shifting allegiances of foreign powers such as the Duchy of Milan and the Kingdom of France.

Fregoso's first dogate (1462–1464) was followed by periods of exile and military leadership, including commanding Genoese fleets against Barbary pirates and engaging in land battles. He reclaimed the dogal office twice more (1478–1480, 1483–1488), often through popular uprisings or strategic alliances, only to be deposed again by internal rivals or external interventions. Simultaneously, he held the influential position of Archbishop of Genoa for 45 years (1453–1498) and later served as Bishop of Ajaccio (1493–1498), leveraging his ecclesiastical authority and wealth to fund his political and military ambitions. His actions frequently blurred the lines between spiritual leadership and worldly power, a common characteristic of high-ranking churchmen of the era.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Paolo Fregoso's career as a three-time Doge and long-serving Archbishop profoundly shaped Genoa's political landscape for nearly five decades, contributing to its chronic instability while also maintaining its maritime power. His actions reflect the broader struggles of Italian city-states against internal factionalism and encroaching foreign powers at the close of the 15th century.
